n: Complete mole: cluster of grape-like vesicles

ww.Partial hydatidiform mole: Partial mole has swollen villi only in part, mixed with normal villi, and often an abnormal fetus or amnion. This specimen is a mass of translucent grape-like vesicles throughout, with no fetal tissue visible, the pattern of a complete mole.
ww.Hydropic abortion (non-molar): Hydropic abortion is a miscarriage with mildly swollen villi, usually small and pale and mixed with clot and fetal tissue. The vesicles here are uniform, translucent, fluid-filled spheres several millimeters wide that dominate the specimen, far beyond mild edema.
ww.Choriocarcinoma of the uterus: Choriocarcinoma forms a soft, dark, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass with no villi, since it is made of sheets of trophoblast. This specimen is pale and translucent, built of fluid-filled vesicles joined by thin strands, and has no solid hemorrhagic tumor.
ww.Echinococcus hydatid cyst: Echinococcus hydatid cysts are parasitic cysts, usually in liver or lung, with a thick white laminated wall and daughter cysts inside. The vesicles here are thin-walled swollen villi joined by fine tissue strands, not parasite cysts.

look: Look at the mass of round, translucent, fluid-filled vesicles of different sizes, joined by thin glistening strands of tissue. Each vesicle is a chorionic villus swollen by edema, and together they look like a cluster of grapes. No fetus or normal placenta is visible in the field. Grape-like vesicles with no embryo are the gross appearance of a complete hydatidiform mole.

findings: Grape-like vesicles: rounded, translucent, thin-walled vesicles a few millimeters wide fill the field, because every villus is swollen by edema into a fluid-filled sac and lacks functioning fetal vessels.
Connecting strands: thin, glistening strands of tissue stretch between the vesicles near the center, showing that the vesicles hang together on villous stalks like grapes on a vine.
Large vesicle, top right: one translucent dome is much larger than its neighbors, showing how widely the size of the swollen villi varies within a single mole.
Red-brown flecks: scattered rust-colored spots of old blood lie between the vesicles, in line with the vaginal bleeding that is the commonest presenting sign of a molar pregnancy.

ann.l: These rounded, translucent vesicles fill the field. In a complete mole, every chorionic villus becomes hydropic—swollen by edema into a fluid-filled sac—because there are no functioning fetal vessels to drain the fluid. This creates the classic 'bunch of grapes' appearance seen on gross examination.

Thin, glistening strands of tissue stretch between the vesicles. These represent the remnants of the villous stalks. Their presence confirms that the vesicles are not independent cysts but are part of a branching placental structure, hanging together like grapes on a vine.

This large, translucent dome is significantly bigger than its neighbors. The degree of villous swelling varies widely within a single molar pregnancy. While some villi remain small, others can grow to over a centimeter in diameter, contributing to the characteristic heterogeneous, cystic appearance.

Scattered rust-colored spots of old blood are visible between the vesicles. This hemorrhage occurs as the molar tissue separates from the decidua. Clinically it shows as vaginal bleeding, the most common presenting symptom of a hydatidiform mole.
